items.sentence: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models Published 13 October 2026 Reading time 8 min Topics claude How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models I work on Claude.

It’s an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn’t considered, didn’t think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try.

Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, “astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others”.
Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying — it’s addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I’ve built.

Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they’re good for beyond asking “What is the capital of France” or “Can you make this email sound less angry”.

I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it.
Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I’ll skip this one.
Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task.
Rather than operating at the task’s layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems.
Altitude We often flippantly call this “letting the model operate at a higher abstraction”.
When you give the model a task, it’s executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want.
You’re at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR).
The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors.

Insist on the same instruments used by the best in the industry: When prompted to act like a professional, models often switch vocabulary without actually switching methods.
Challenge what you know: Especially in business, a lot of things we believe to be true are rough approximations of reality.
This isn’t a particularly unique insight, every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents.
It might be useful to employ an adversarial “red team”, too, so let’s bring in a short seller and a forensic accountant.
It is easy to accidentally engage in role play, which will make your transcript weirder without improving the actual outcome.
Plenty of tools make this possible and I recommend that you use one.
While researching the problem of ambition, I learned that psychology has a name for this: self-efficacy.
Stripe founder Patrick Collison maintains a “Fast” list, chronicling the many things humans have accomplished when given both audacious goals and tight deadlines.
